newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Flashy paint jobs mask new truck safety features.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Flashy paint jobs mask new truck safety features.

text.p: Impressive paintwork and shiny chrome on the latest generation of new buses and trucks mask new features under the exteriors aimed at making commercial vehicles safer.
Spectacular accidents during the last few years involving motor coaches and trucks, including a number of deadly highway crashes, have raised public concerns.

Truck and bus manufacturers heard the uproar and have begun implementing new features -- from air bags and larger windows to anti-lock braking systems -- as well as bringing in comfort features to reduce driver fatigue, a major cause of accidents.

Driver seats have been improved to take out the "bounce", with many seats giving the feel that the driver is floating. Seatbelts have been attached to the seats instead of the cab, reducing the chance of serious injury in crashes.

"There is an emerging awareness that trucks and buses need to be safer and that helps keep the public safer," said Ralph Kisiel, truck editor at Automotive News, the bible of the U.S. automobile and commercial vehicle industry.
European law has for some years required that commercial vehicles have anti-lock brakes. A U.S. law will require the sophisticated brakes on new vehicles beginning in early 1997.
Although airbags are not yet mandatory for vehicles in Europe and the U.S., many manufacturers offer them as optional.
NEW SAFETY FEATURES ARE JUST THE BEGINNING
Such safety features are just the beginning.

Industry executives see the next generation of trucks offering brake-by-wire systems, high-intensity headlamps, collision avoidance systems, daytime running lights, adaptive cruise control to adjust to traffic conditions and computerised transmissions to keep a driver's attention on the road.
Development of brake-by-wire systems, where drivers will have faster response when they hit the brake pedal, is one of the top future projects.
Under the system, commands for braking are transmitted electronically to each brake instead of through hydraulics or air brakes, eliminating delays.
In addition, leading makers such as Mercedes-Benz, Scania, Volvo and Iveco are pouring millions of dollars into research to improve their comfort, turning some vehicles into "apartments on wheels".
Mercedes-Benz, which has the top European market share for commercial vehicles, recently unveiled its new Actros heavy duty truck, which it calls "one of the most comfortable work places in Europe".
The "cab-over" truck, where the engine is placed under the passenger compartment, offers a new braking system to reduce stopping distances, in some cases equalling passenger vehicles.
The truck also offers state-of-the-art ergonomic design with a cockpit-style arrangement where all controls are within easy reach. Interior noise has also been reduced with sound-dampening material.
Switches for ventilation, heating and air conditioning are within easy reach of the driver, while a cassette/CD radio even has an infra-red remote control to keep hands on the wheel.
A person nearly two metres (over six feet) tall can stand upright in the cab, with some models offering such options as a microwave, television and a bed for long-haul drivers.
"We talked with a number of drivers and they wanted the cab to be bigger and more comfortable," said Hartmut Marwitz, director of Mercedes' truck engineering division.
"We want to give a driver a better chance at not being injured by raising the level of safety," Marwitz said.
CONCERNS ABOUT COST
But new safety equipment comes at a cost, one that many trucking and bus companies are not willing to pay for extras on vehicles that can each often cost well above 150,000 marks ($97,490).
In addition, the average lifespan of a commercial vehicle is some 10 to 15 years, meaning new safety features will take several years longer to be implemented than in passenger cars.
"That's the eternal dilemma," said Jens Peter Raahauge, director of communications at Italian truck maker Iveco SpA, of the requirement for manufacturers to keep prices competitive.
"A truck has a cost and fleet owners these days are tremendously conscious of what they are willing to pay. They want safe vehicles but at the lowest cost," he said.
Some manufacturers say new technology must still prove its value, particularly with collision avoidance systems.

Mercedes' Marwitz said the systems must be improved to be able to recognise objects and whether they are moving and present imminent danger to the vehicle. Such systems could then take over control of the truck, as happens in aircraft.

"These systems have to be very precise about what objects are ahead," Marwitz said, noting that automatic braking systems could be linked to the system. "The brain can sometimes be too slow in reacting."
